Package com.egradx.auth.security

Class EgradxAccessGuard

java.lang.Object
com.egradx.auth.security.EgradxAccessGuard
@Component("egradxAccessGuard") public class EgradxAccessGuard extends Object
The @PreAuthorize SpEL bean (@egradxAccessGuard.…) for the SDK's own REST controllers in com.egradx.auth.web.

Deliberately scoped to those controllers only, not the services underneath them (EgradxRoleService, EgradxUserService, EgradxOrganizationService). Those are the in-process API a host app calls directly — under whatever access control the host app has already applied to its own adapter, and sometimes with no SecurityContextHolder authentication at all (e.g. DataSeeder running at startup). Putting this check there instead would have broken exactly that.

This enforces the tenant boundary only: a caller may act on their own organization, and the platform organization's members may act on any. What a given member is allowed to do within their own organization is a separate question, answered by the hasAuthority('egradx.…') half of the same @PreAuthorize expressions — see EgradxAuthorities. Both halves are needed: the authority check alone would let an administrator of one organization operate on another (they hold egradx.role.manage either way), and this check alone would let any member of an organization administer it.

  • Method Details

    • isPlatformSession

      public boolean isPlatformSession()
      Whether this session is scoped to the platform organization.

      egradx-auth's own endpoints no longer use this — they gate on hasAuthority('egradx.organization.*') instead, which is the stronger check because EgradxRoleService reserves those authorities to the platform organization's own roles. It stays public for host apps that want a platform-only endpoint of their own without inventing an authority for it.
